claim: Melanoma cells undergo fast amoeboid (leader bleb-based) migration requiring a single large bleb for migration.
source: Melanoma cells have been shown to undergo fast amoeboid (leader bleb-based) migration, requiring a single large bleb for migration.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract as a known phenomenon that forms the basis of the study.

claim: Leader blebs contain a rapid flow of cortical actin that drives the cell forward.
source: In leader blebs, is a rapid flow of cortical actin that drives the cell forward.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract and supported by imaging data in Figure 1B.

claim: Co-depleting cofilin-1 and ADF leads to a large increase in cortical actin.
source: Using RNAi, we find that co-depleting cofilin-1 and actin depolymerizing factor (ADF) led to a large increase in cortical actin, suggesting that both proteins regulate cortical actin.
evidence: This is supported by flow cytometry data showing F-actin levels in Figure 3C.

claim: Severing factors can promote contractility through the regulation of actin architecture.
source: Furthermore, severing factors can promote contractility through the regulation of actin architecture.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract and supported by cell stiffness measurements in Figure 5A.

claim: RNAi of cofilin-1 but not ADF leads to a significant decrease in cell stiffness.
source: However, RNAi of cofilin-1 but not ADF led to a significant decrease in cell stiffness.
evidence: This is supported by gel sandwich assay data in Figure 5A showing increased compressibility (decreased stiffness) after cofilin-1 depletion.

claim: Cofilin-1 is enriched at leader bleb necks.
source: We found cofilin-1 to be enriched at leader bleb necks, whereas RNAi of cofilin-1 and ADF reduced bleb sizes and the frequency of motile cells.
evidence: This is supported by imaging data in Figure 2I showing EGFP-cofilin-1 localization.

claim: RNAi of cofilin-1 and ADF reduces bleb sizes.
source: We found cofilin-1 to be enriched at leader bleb necks, whereas RNAi of cofilin-1 and ADF reduced bleb sizes and the frequency of motile cells.
evidence: This is supported by quantitative data in Figure 2B-C showing reduced bleb areas.

claim: RNAi of cofilin-1 and ADF reduces the frequency of motile cells.
source: We found cofilin-1 to be enriched at leader bleb necks, whereas RNAi of cofilin-1 and ADF reduced bleb sizes and the frequency of motile cells.
evidence: This is supported by cell tracking data in Figure 1E-F showing reduced percentage of highly motile cells.

claim: Cells without cofilin-1 and ADF have blebs with abnormally long necks.
source: Strikingly, cells without cofilin-1 and ADF had blebs with abnormally long necks.
evidence: This is supported by imaging data in Figure 2A and quantification in Figure 2D.

claim: Many blebs in cells without cofilin-1 and ADF fail to retract.
source: Many of these blebs failed to retract and displayed slow actin turnover.
evidence: This is supported by data in Figure 2E showing ~60% of blebs with elongated necks never retract.

claim: Blebs in cells without cofilin-1 and ADF display slow actin turnover.
source: Many of these blebs failed to retract and displayed slow actin turnover.
evidence: This is supported by photoactivation data in Figure 4G showing increased t1/2 for actin turnover.

claim: Cofilin-1 and ADF are actin remodeling factors required for fast amoeboid migration.
source: Collectively, our data identifies cofilin-1 and ADF as actin remodeling factors required for fast amoeboid migration.
evidence: This is the main conclusion supported by multiple lines of experimental evidence throughout the manuscript.

claim: Cell migration requires tight spatiotemporal control of the filamentous-actin (F-actin) cytoskeleton.
source: Cell migration requires tight spatiotemporal control of the filamentous-actin (F-actin) cytoskeleton.
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge in the introduction.

claim: For mesenchymal migration, actin assembly/disassembly and myosin contraction must occur within specific regions of the cell.
source: For mesenchymal migration, actin assembly/disassembly and myosin contraction must occur within specific regions of the cell (Pollard and Borisy, 2003).
evidence: This is supported by citation to prior work.

claim: The mechanisms by which mesenchymal cells coordinate actin assembly/disassembly and myosin contraction are reasonably well understood.
source: Relative to other, recently described modes of migration, the mechanisms by which mesenchymal cells coordinate these processes are reasonably well understood.
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge in the introduction.

claim: In amoeboid cells, the mechanisms conferring spatiotemporal control of the F-actin cytoskeleton are not well known.
source: Whereas, in amoeboid cells, which migrate using intracellular-driven protrusions of the plasma membrane (PM) or blebs, the mechanisms conferring spatiotemporal control of the F-actin cytoskeleton are not well known.
evidence: This is stated as a knowledge gap in the introduction.

claim: Amoeboid cells migrate using intracellular-driven protrusions of the plasma membrane or blebs.
source: Whereas, in amoeboid cells, which migrate using intracellular-driven protrusions of the plasma membrane (PM) or blebs, the mechanisms conferring spatiotemporal control of the F-actin cytoskeleton are not well known.
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge in the introduction.

claim: In response to tissue confinement, cancer cells frequently undergo phenotypic transitions, including to fast amoeboid migration.
source: We and others discovered that in response to tissue confinement, cancer cells frequently undergo phenotypic transitions, including to what has been termed 'fast amoeboid migration' (Logue et al., 2015; Liu et al., 2015; Ruprecht et al., 2015; Bergert et al., 2015; Mistriotis et al., 2019; Wisniewski et al., 2020).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations to prior work.

claim: A hallmark of amoeboid migration is the presence of blebs, which form as a result of PM-cortical actin separation.
source: A hallmark of amoeboid migration is the presence of blebs, which form as a result of PM-cortical actin separation (Charras et al., 2008).
evidence: This is supported by citation to prior work.

claim: Blebs are typically rapidly retracted following the reassembly of cortical actin on bleb membranes and the recruitment of myosin.
source: Typically, blebs are rapidly retracted following the reassembly of cortical actin on bleb membranes and the recruitment of myosin (Charras et al., 2008).
evidence: This is supported by citation to prior work.

claim: During fast amoeboid migration, cells form a very large and stable bleb.
source: However, during fast amoeboid migration, cells form a very large and stable bleb.
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge and supported by imaging data in Figure 1A.

claim: Within leader blebs, cortical actin flows from the bleb tip to the neck, which separates leader blebs from the cell body.
source: Within these blebs, is a cortical actin network that flows from the bleb tip to the neck, which separates leader blebs from the cell body (Logue et al., 2015; Liu et al., 2015; Ruprecht et al., 2015; Bergert et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by citations and imaging data in Figure 1B.

claim: Flowing cortical actin together with non-specific friction provides the motive force for cell movement during fast amoeboid migration.
source: Together with non-specific friction, flowing cortical actin provides the motive force for cell movement (Ruprecht et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by citation to prior work.

claim: Myosin is enriched at the neck of leader blebs.
source: Previous studies have demonstrated that myosin is enriched at the neck of leader blebs.
evidence: This is supported by citations and imaging data in Figure 1C showing EGFP-RLC localization.

claim: Myosin at the leader bleb neck is required for rapid cortical actin flow.
source: Indeed, the myosin at this location has been shown to be required for rapid cortical actin flow (Liu et al., 2015; Ruprecht et al., 2015; Bergert et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior work.

claim: What drives the disassembly of F-actin at the neck to replenish the pool of G-actin at the leader bleb tip is unknown.
source: However, what drives the disassembly of F-actin at the neck to replenish the pool of G-actin at the leader bleb tip is unknown.
evidence: This is stated as a knowledge gap that motivates the study.

claim: Actin disassembly factors within leader blebs play a pivotal role in replenishing the pool of G-actin at the leader bleb tip.
source: Thus, we hypothesize that actin disassembly factors within leader blebs play a pivotal role in this process.
evidence: This is stated as the hypothesis of the study.

claim: In mesenchymal cells, retrograde actin flow is driven by both myosin contraction and actin disassembly.
source: Similarly, in mesenchymal cells, retrograde actin flow is driven by both myosin contraction and actin disassembly, the latter of which is accelerated by the actin depolymerizing factor (ADF)/cofilin family of severing factors (Bravo-Cordero et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by citation to prior work.

claim: Actin disassembly in mesenchymal cells is accelerated by the ADF/cofilin family of severing factors.
source: Similarly, in mesenchymal cells, retrograde actin flow is driven by both myosin contraction and actin disassembly, the latter of which is accelerated by the actin depolymerizing factor (ADF)/cofilin family of severing factors (Bravo-Cordero et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by citation to prior work.

claim: Severing by ADF/cofilin depends on inducing a structural change within the actin filament.
source: Severing depends on ADF/cofilin inducing a structural change within the actin filament, an activity known to be repressed by LIM kinase (LIMK) phosphorylation on Ser 3 (Yang et al., 1998).
evidence: This is supported by citation to prior work.

claim: ADF/cofilin severing activity is repressed by LIMK phosphorylation on Ser 3.
source: Severing depends on ADF/cofilin inducing a structural change within the actin filament, an activity known to be repressed by LIM kinase (LIMK) phosphorylation on Ser 3 (Yang et al., 1998).
evidence: This is supported by citation to prior work.

claim: The consequence of actin severing by ADF/cofilin is variable, depending on the availability of barbed end capping proteins.
source: However, the consequence of actin severing is variable, depending on the availability of barbed end capping proteins.
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge and supported by citation.

claim: At a sufficiently high level of capping proteins, new barbed ends are capped, promoting actin disassembly from new pointed ends.
source: At a sufficiently high level, new barbed ends are capped, promoting actin disassembly from new pointed ends (Wioland et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by citation to prior work.

claim: If barbed ends are left uncapped after severing, increased polymerization from new barbed ends may occur.
source: Conversely, if left uncapped, increased polymerization from new barbed ends may occur (Wioland et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by citation to prior work.

claim: The effects of ADF/cofilin on actin severing are concentration dependent, where low and high levels of ADF/cofilin sever and stabilize actin filaments, respectively.
source: The effects of ADF/cofilin on actin severing is also concentration dependent, where low and high levels of ADF/cofilin sever and stabilize actin filaments, respectively (Andrianantoandro and Pollard, 2006).
evidence: This is supported by citation to prior work.

claim: ADF/cofilin can regulate actin architecture by competing for F-actin binding and other mechanisms.
source: Additionally, by competing for F-actin binding (e.g., Arp2/3) and other mechanisms, ADF/cofilin can regulate actin architecture (Chan et al., 2009; Gressin et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior work.

claim: The effects of ADF/cofilin on cortical actin are less certain, as the focus of many studies has been on the actin within lamellipodia.
source: The effects of ADF/cofilin on cortical actin are even less certain, as the focus of many studies has been on the actin within lamellipodia.
evidence: This is stated as a knowledge gap in the introduction.

claim: Wiggan et al. previously reported bleb defects in HeLa cells depleted of actin severing factors.
source: Although Wiggan et al. have previously reported bleb defects in HeLa cells depleted of actin severing factors, the role of ADF and cofilin-1 in regulating the cortical actomyosin flow in fast amoeboid cells has not been determined (Wiggan et al., 2012).
evidence: This is supported by citation to prior work.

claim: The role of ADF and cofilin-1 in regulating the cortical actomyosin flow in fast amoeboid cells has not been determined.
source: Although Wiggan et al. have previously reported bleb defects in HeLa cells depleted of actin severing factors, the role of ADF and cofilin-1 in regulating the cortical actomyosin flow in fast amoeboid cells has not been determined (Wiggan et al., 2012).
evidence: This is stated as a knowledge gap that motivates the study.

claim: ADF and cofilin-1, together, are required for the rapid disassembly of incoming cortical actin at leader bleb necks.
source: By combining an in vitro assay for the precise confinement of cells with quantitative imaging approaches, we report that ADF and cofilin-1, together, are required for the rapid disassembly of incoming cortical actin at leader bleb necks.
evidence: This is the main finding supported by multiple experimental approaches including CALI and photoactivation assays.

claim: Under conditions of confinement, melanoma and lung adenocarcinoma cells depleted of both ADF and cofilin-1 display dramatic defects in bleb morphology and dynamics.
source: Under conditions of confinement, we find that melanoma and lung adenocarcinoma cells depleted of both proteins display dramatic defects in bleb morphology and dynamics.
evidence: This is supported by imaging data in Figures 2A and 2F-G.

claim: Cells without ADF and cofilin-1 cannot undergo LBBM.
source: Consequently, cells without ADF and cofilin-1 cannot undergo LBBM.
evidence: This is supported by cell tracking data in Figure 1E-H showing reduced motility.

claim: The properties of the cortical actin network in spherical cells correlate with LBBM.
source: Previous work by us and others has shown that the properties of the cortical actin network in spherical cells correlate with LBBM (Logue et al., 2015; Liu et al., 2015; Bergert et al., 2012).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior work.

claim: In spherical cells, actin is predominantly cortical.
source: In spherical cells, actin is predominantly cortical and endogenous cofilin-1 is diffuse throughout the cytoplasm with some enrichment at the cell periphery (Figure 3B).
evidence: This is supported by imaging data in Figure 3B.

claim: In spherical cells, endogenous cofilin-1 is diffuse throughout the cytoplasm with some enrichment at the cell periphery.
source: In spherical cells, actin is predominantly cortical and endogenous cofilin-1 is diffuse throughout the cytoplasm with some enrichment at the cell periphery (Figure 3B).
evidence: This is supported by imaging data in Figure 3B.

claim: In cells depleted of cofilin-1, F-actin levels were increased by ~10%.
source: In cells depleted of cofilin-1, F-actin levels were increased by ~10%, whereas depletion of ADF did not lead to a significant change in the level of F-actin (Figure 3C).
evidence: This is supported by flow cytometry data in Figure 3C.

claim: Depletion of ADF did not lead to a significant change in the level of F-actin.
source: In cells depleted of cofilin-1, F-actin levels were increased by ~10%, whereas depletion of ADF did not lead to a significant change in the level of F-actin (Figure 3C).
evidence: This is supported by flow cytometry data in Figure 3C.

claim: Depleting ADF with cofilin-1 increases F-actin levels by ~30%.
source: Interestingly, depleting ADF with cofilin-1 had the largest effect, increasing F-actin levels by ~30% (Figure 3C).
evidence: This is supported by flow cytometry data in Figure 3C.

claim: Serine 3 of cofilin-1 is phosphorylated by LIMK, inhibiting its severing activity.
source: Serine 3 of cofilin-1 is phosphorylated by LIMK, inhibiting its severing activity (Yang et al., 1998).
evidence: This is supported by citation to prior work.

claim: In cells depleted of endogenous ADF and cofilin-1, transfection of EGFP-cofilin-1 reduced the level of F-actin to levels similar to control.
source: In cells depleted of endogenous ADF and cofilin-1, transfection of EGFP-cofilin-1 reduced the level of F-actin to levels similar to control (non-target; Figure 3D).
evidence: This is supported by flow cytometry data in Figure 3D.

claim: F-actin was restored to near control levels by transfection of EGFP-cofilin-1 (S3A; constitutively active).
source: Similarly, F-actin was restored to near control levels by transfection of EGFP-cofilin-1 (S3A; constitutively active), whereas transfection of EGFP-cofilin-1 (S3E; constitutively inactive) led to an increased level of F-actin (Figure 3D).
evidence: This is supported by flow cytometry data in Figure 3D.

claim: Transfection of EGFP-cofilin-1 (S3E; constitutively inactive) led to an increased level of F-actin.
source: Similarly, F-actin was restored to near control levels by transfection of EGFP-cofilin-1 (S3A; constitutively active), whereas transfection of EGFP-cofilin-1 (S3E; constitutively inactive) led to an increased level of F-actin (Figure 3D).
evidence: This is supported by flow cytometry data in Figure 3D.

claim: Increasing levels of EGFP-cofilin-1 correlate with reductions in F-actin.
source: Additionally, in comparison to EGFP alone, increasing levels of EGFP-cofilin-1 correlated with reductions in F-actin (Figure 3E).
evidence: This is supported by flow cytometry data in Figure 3E.

claim: Cortical actin levels are regulated by ADF and cofilin-1 severing.
source: Thus, cortical actin levels are regulated by ADF and cofilin-1 severing.
evidence: This is inferred from the rescue experiments with wild-type and mutant cofilin-1 constructs.

claim: In lamellipodia, cofilin-1 severing promotes actin polymerization at new barbed ends.
source: In lamellipodia, cofilin-1 severing promotes actin polymerization at new barbed ends, whereas in the lamella, actin is de-polymerized at new pointed ends (Bravo-Cordero et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by citation to prior work.

claim: In the lamella, actin is de-polymerized at new pointed ends after cofilin-1 severing.
source: In lamellipodia, cofilin-1 severing promotes actin polymerization at new barbed ends, whereas in the lamella, actin is de-polymerized at new pointed ends (Bravo-Cordero et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by citation to prior work.

claim: The prevalence of polymerization vs. depolymerization outcomes after severing depends on the concentration of capping proteins.
source: The prevalence of each outcome has been proposed to depend on the concentration of capping proteins (Wioland et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by citation to prior work.

claim: In cells depleted of cofilin-1, there was a more than ~50% increase in the level of cortical barbed ends.
source: In cells depleted of cofilin-1, we observed a more than ~50% increase the level of cortical barbed ends, whereas depleting ADF marginally increased the level of cortical barbed ends (Figure 3G).
evidence: This is supported by barbed end assay data in Figure 3G.

claim: Depleting ADF marginally increased the level of cortical barbed ends.
source: In cells depleted of cofilin-1, we observed a more than ~50% increase the level of cortical barbed ends, whereas depleting ADF marginally increased the level of cortical barbed ends (Figure 3G).
evidence: This is supported by barbed end assay data in Figure 3G.

claim: Depleting cells of both ADF and cofilin-1 appeared to have an additive effect, increasing the level of cortical barbed ends by ~100%.
source: Depleting cells of both proteins appeared to have an additive effect, increasing the level of cortical barbed ends by ~100% (Figure 3G).
evidence: This is supported by barbed end assay data in Figure 3G.

claim: In cells depleted of ADF and cofilin-1, transfection of EGFP-cofilin-1 was sufficient to restore cortical barbed ends to a level similar to control.
source: However, in cells depleted of ADF and cofilin-1, transfection of EGFP-cofilin-1 was sufficient to restore cortical barbed ends to a level similar to control (Figure 3H).
evidence: This is supported by barbed end assay data in Figure 3H.

claim: ADF and cofilin-1 regulate cortical actin levels by promoting the de-polymerization of actin at newly formed pointed ends.
source: Collectively, these results suggest that ADF and cofilin-1 regulate cortical actin levels by promoting the de-polymerization of actin at newly formed pointed ends.
evidence: This is inferred from the barbed end assay results showing increased barbed ends after depletion.

claim: Lasting changes in the F/G-actin ratio can have a range of effects on cellular physiology.
source: Lasting changes in the F/G-actin ratio, such as occurs during RNAi of ADF and/or cofilin-1, can have a range of effects on cellular physiology.
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge.

claim: In cells depleted of ADF and cofilin-1, SuperNova-cofilin-1 is predominantly observed at leader bleb necks.
source: In cells depleted of ADF and cofilin-1, SuperNova-cofilin-1 is predominantly observed at leader bleb necks (Figure 4A).
evidence: This is supported by imaging data in Figure 4A.

claim: After 1 min of intense red light irradiation, ~50% of SuperNova-cofilin-1 is destroyed.
source: After 1 min of intense red light irradiation, we found that ~50% of SuperNova-cofilin-1 is destroyed, as indicated by a reduction in red fluorescence (Figure 4A).
evidence: This is supported by quantitative data in Figure 4A.

claim: An accumulation of actin and the elongation of leader bleb necks occurs within minutes of inactivating cofilin-1.
source: Using LifeAct-mEmerald for monitoring actin dynamics, we observed an accumulation of actin and the elongation of leader bleb necks within minutes of inactivating cofilin-1 (Figure 4B and Video 7).
evidence: This is supported by imaging data in Figure 4B and Video 7.

claim: After inactivating SuperNova-cofilin-1, cortical actin flow rates in leader blebs were reduced by ~50%.
source: Moreover, after inactivating SuperNova-cofilin-1, cortical actin flow rates in leader blebs were reduced by ~50%, whereas irradiation of SuperNova alone did not change actin flow rates (Figure 4C–D and Figure 4—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This is supported by kymograph analysis in Figure 4C-D.

claim: Irradiation of SuperNova alone did not change actin flow rates.
source: Moreover, after inactivating SuperNova-cofilin-1, cortical actin flow rates in leader blebs were reduced by ~50%, whereas irradiation of SuperNova alone did not change actin flow rates (Figure 4C–D and Figure 4—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This is supported by control data in Figure 4—figure supplement 1A.

claim: Cofilin-1 directly regulates the cortical actin in leader blebs.
source: Thus, as demonstrated by CALI, cofilin-1 directly regulates the cortical actin in leader blebs.
evidence: This is inferred from the CALI experiments showing rapid effects on actin flow after cofilin-1 inactivation.

claim: Changes in the cellular F/G-actin ratio can trigger specific transcriptional programs, such as through the activation of the transcription factor, MRTF-A.
source: Because changes in the cellular F/G-actin ratio can trigger specific transcriptional programs, such as through the activation of the transcription factor, MRTF-A, we wanted to determine if the effects we observed on LBBM are a direct result of down-regulating actin severing (Olson and Nordheim, 2010).
evidence: This is supported by citation to prior work.

claim: In cells depleted of ADF and cofilin-1, SuperNova-coflin-1 was sufficient to restore normal bleb morphology and dynamics.
source: In cells depleted of ADF and cofilin-1, SuperNova-coflin-1 was sufficient to restore normal bleb morphology and dynamics.
evidence: This is supported by imaging data showing normal blebs before CALI in Figure 4B.

claim: Within minutes of cofilin-1 inactivation, actin began to accumulate at elongated bleb necks.
source: However, within minutes of cofilin-1 inactivation, actin began to accumulate at elongated bleb necks.
evidence: This is supported by imaging data in Figure 4B.

claim: Depleting ADF or cofilin-1 alone did not have a significant effect on actin turnover rates at bleb necks.
source: While depleting ADF or cofilin-1 alone did not have a significant effect on actin turnover rates, depleting both proteins led to a large increase in the rate of actin turnover at bleb necks.
evidence: This is supported by photoactivation data in Figure 4G.

claim: Depleting both ADF and cofilin-1 led to a large increase in the half-life of actin turnover at bleb necks.
source: While depleting ADF or cofilin-1 alone did not have a significant effect on actin turnover rates, depleting both proteins led to a large increase in the rate of actin turnover at bleb necks.
evidence: This is supported by photoactivation data in Figure 4G showing increased t1/2.

claim: Cofilin-1 has been previously implicated in regulating actomyosin contractility.
source: Cofilin-1 has been previously implicated in regulating actomyosin contractility.
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge.

claim: Cells were found to be less stiff after depleting cofilin-1, as indicated by increased compressibility.
source: As indicated by increased compressibility, cells were found to be less stiff after depleting cofilin-1.
evidence: This is supported by gel sandwich assay data in Figure 5A.

claim: Removing ADF had little effect on cell stiffness.
source: In contrast, removing ADF had little effect on cell stiffness.
evidence: This is supported by gel sandwich assay data in Figure 5A.

claim: Depleting both ADF and cofilin-1 was similar to removing cofilin-1 alone in terms of cell stiffness.
source: Moreover, depleting both ADF and cofilin-1 was similar to removing cofilin-1 alone and could be rescued by an RNAi resistant version of cofilin-1 but not ADF.
evidence: This is supported by gel sandwich assay data in Figure 5A-B.

claim: Cell stiffness defects after ADF and cofilin-1 depletion could be rescued by an RNAi resistant version of cofilin-1 but not ADF.
source: Moreover, depleting both ADF and cofilin-1 was similar to removing cofilin-1 alone and could be rescued by an RNAi resistant version of cofilin-1 but not ADF.
evidence: This is supported by rescue experiments in Figure 5B-C.

claim: Cofilin-1 may be particularly important to support actomyosin contractility.
source: Therefore, cofilin-1 may be particularly important to support actomyosin contractility.
evidence: This is inferred from the stiffness and rescue experiments.

claim: Cofilin-1 has been shown to support myosin contractility through optimizing actin filament lengths and de-branching.
source: In line with this notion, cofilin-1 has been shown to support myosin contractility through optimizing actin filament lengths and de-branching (Chan et al., 2009; Chugh et al., 2017; Ennomani et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior work.

claim: Removing ADF and/or cofilin-1 does not appear to affect signaling to myosin, as indicated by the lack of any change in pRLC levels or localization.
source: As indicated by the lack of any change in pRLC levels or localization, removing these proteins does not appear to effect signaling to myosin.
evidence: This is supported by immunofluorescence data in Figure 5D-E.

claim: Depleting ADF and cofilin-1 leads to the elongation of leader bleb necks, which are decorated with myosin.
source: In confined cells, depleting ADF and cofilin-1 leads to the elongation of leader bleb necks, which are decorated with myosin (EGFP-RLC; Figure 5F).
evidence: This is supported by imaging data in Figure 5F.

claim: Within minutes of SuperNova-cofilin-1 inactivation, myosin accumulates at leader bleb necks.
source: Indeed, within minutes of SuperNova-cofilin-1 inactivation, we observed myosin accumulating at leader bleb necks (EGFP-RLC; Figure 5G and Video 8).
evidence: This is supported by imaging data in Figure 5G and Video 8.

claim: The flow of myosin toward leader bleb necks was significantly impeded after cofilin-1 inactivation.
source: Additionally, the flow of myosin toward leader bleb necks was significantly impeded after cofilin-1 inactivation, as determined by tracking individual myosin minifilaments (Figure 5H).
evidence: This is supported by quantitative tracking data in Figure 5H.

claim: ADF may be particularly important for actin turnover.
source: While ADF may be particularly important for actin turnover, these results point to cofilin-1 as having important roles in both actin turnover and myosin contractility at leader bleb necks.
evidence: This is inferred from the differential effects of ADF vs. cofilin-1 depletion on various parameters.

claim: Cofilin-1 has important roles in both actin turnover and myosin contractility at leader bleb necks.
source: While ADF may be particularly important for actin turnover, these results point to cofilin-1 as having important roles in both actin turnover and myosin contractility at leader bleb necks.
evidence: This is inferred from the multiple effects of cofilin-1 depletion on actin dynamics and cell stiffness.

claim: ADF and cofilin-1 play key roles during LBBM by optimizing actin disassembly and myosin contractility at bleb necks.
source: Thus, our data are consistent with a model whereby ADF and cofilin-1 play key roles during LBBM. More specifically, we assert that ADF and cofilin-1, together, optimize actin disassembly and myosin contractility at bleb necks (Figure 6, top).
evidence: This is the main conclusion of the study supported by multiple lines of evidence.

claim: In the absence of ADF and cofilin-1, incoming cortical actin fails to disassemble and accumulates with myosin at the elongated necks of persistent blebs.
source: Whereas, in the absence of these proteins, incoming cortical actin fails to disassemble and accumulates with myosin at the elongated necks of persistent blebs (Figure 6, below).
evidence: This is supported by imaging data showing actin and myosin accumulation at elongated necks.

claim: Rapid cortical actin flows are essential for confined (leader bleb-based) migration.
source: Collectively, this study further points to rapid (cortical) actin flows as being essential for confined (leader bleb-based) migration.
evidence: This is inferred from the observation that disrupting actin flow by depleting ADF and cofilin-1 inhibits LBBM.

claim: Many cancer cells have been shown to undergo LBBM.
source: This is significant as many cancer cells have been shown to undergo LBBM (Logue et al., 2015; Liu et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior work.

claim: In melanoma cells, ADF appears to augment the activity of cofilin-1 at bleb necks.
source: This work also reveals an unanticipated role for ADF. In melanoma cells, ADF appears to augment the activity of cofilin-1 at bleb necks.
evidence: This is inferred from the additive effects of depleting both proteins on various parameters.

claim: ADF and cofilin-1 are thought to have redundant or overlapping roles.
source: Largely, ADF and cofilin-1 are thought to have redundant or overlapping roles (Hotulainen et al., 2005).
evidence: This is supported by citation to prior work.

claim: ADF has been shown to have significant monomer sequestering activity.
source: However, ADF has been shown to have significant monomer sequestering activity (Chen et al., 2004).
evidence: This is supported by citation to prior work.

claim: In the absence of both ADF and cofilin-1, dampened actin severing coupled with uncontrolled filament elongation contributes to the severe phenotypes observed.
source: We speculate that, in the absence of both proteins, dampened actin severing coupled with uncontrolled filament elongation contributes to the severe phenotypes we observe.
evidence: This is stated as speculation based on the observed phenotypes and known functions of the proteins.

claim: The dissemination of melanoma tumors is likely to be blocked by the simultaneous inhibition of ADF and cofilin-1.
source: Thus, the dissemination of melanoma tumors is likely to be blocked by the simultaneous inhibition of ADF and cofilin-1.
evidence: This is speculated based on the finding that depleting both proteins inhibits LBBM.

claim: Actin severing by ADF and cofilin-1 can be regulated by a number of functional interactions, such as with Aip1 and cyclase-associated protein 1.
source: As actin severing by ADF and cofilin-1 can be regulated by a number of functional interactions, such as with Aip1 and cyclase-associated protein 1, future work will endeavor to determine the contribution of these factors in regulating the cortical actomyosin flow in fast amoeboid cells (Bertling et al., 2004; Nadkarni and Brieher, 2014; Chen et al., 2015; Shekhar et al., 2019; Kotila et al., 2019).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior work.

claim: In melanoma A375 cells, both ADF and cofilin-1 are expressed, with cofilin-1 mRNA levels being threefold higher.
source: In melanoma A375 cells, a widely used cell line for the study of amoeboid migration, both ADF and cofilin-1 are expressed, with cofilin-1 mRNA levels being threefold higher (Figure 1—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: This is supported by qRT-PCR data in Figure 1—figure supplement 1B.

claim: Cells depleted of cofilin-1 were significantly less motile.
source: By manually tracking the movement of cells over time, we found that cells depleted of cofilin-1 were significantly less motile (Figure 1E–H and Figure 1—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: This is supported by cell tracking data in Figure 1E-H.

claim: The adhesive transmigration of cells through small pores was hindered after depleting cofilin-1.
source: Additionally, the adhesive transmigration of cells through small pores was hindered after depleting cofilin-1 (Figure 1—figure supplement 1D).
evidence: This is supported by transmigration assay data in Figure 1—figure supplement 1D.

claim: Depleting cells of ADF led to a slight reduction in the number of highly motile cells.
source: Depleting cells of ADF led to a slight reduction in the number of highly motile cells (Figure 1E–H and Figure 1—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: This is supported by cell tracking data in Figure 1E-H.

claim: Depleting cells of both ADF and cofilin-1 appeared to have an additive effect on reducing LBBM.
source: Strikingly, depleting cells of both ADF and cofilin-1 appeared to have an additive effect on reducing LBBM, whereas the adhesive transmigration of cells through small pores did not display this additive behavior and was not affected by ADF depletion (Figure 1E–H and Figure 1—figure supplement 1D).
evidence: This is supported by cell tracking data in Figure 1E-H.

claim: The adhesive transmigration of cells through small pores did not display additive behavior after depleting both ADF and cofilin-1.
source: Strikingly, depleting cells of both ADF and cofilin-1 appeared to have an additive effect on reducing LBBM, whereas the adhesive transmigration of cells through small pores did not display this additive behavior and was not affected by ADF depletion (Figure 1E–H and Figure 1—figure supplement 1D).
evidence: This is supported by transmigration assay data in Figure 1—figure supplement 1D.

claim: ADF and cofilin-1 play non-overlapping roles during LBBM.
source: These results suggest that these proteins play non-overlapping roles during LBBM (Figure 1E–H).
evidence: This is inferred from the additive effects of depleting both proteins.

claim: Transfection of EGFP-cofilin-1 into cells depleted of both ADF and cofilin-1 was insufficient to restore LBBM.
source: In agreement with this concept, transfection of EGFP-cofilin-1 into cells depleted of both proteins was insufficient to restore LBBM (Figure 1E–I).
evidence: This is supported by rescue experiment data in Figure 1E-I.

claim: Depleting cells of cofilin-1 reduced the area of the largest bleb by ~15% of control.
source: This analysis revealed that depleting cells of cofilin-1 reduced the area of the largest bleb by ~15% of control while depleting cells of both ADF and cofilin-1 reduced the area of the largest bleb by ~40% of control (non-targeting; Figure 2A–B and Videos 3–5).
evidence: This is supported by quantitative data in Figure 2B.

claim: Depleting cells of both ADF and cofilin-1 reduced the area of the largest bleb by ~40% of control.
source: This analysis revealed that depleting cells of cofilin-1 reduced the area of the largest bleb by ~15% of control while depleting cells of both ADF and cofilin-1 reduced the area of the largest bleb by ~40% of control (non-targeting; Figure 2A–B and Videos 3–5).
evidence: This is supported by quantitative data in Figure 2B.

claim: In cells depleted of both ADF and cofilin-1, ~30% of cells displayed blebs with elongated necks.
source: Strikingly, in cells depleted of both ADF and cofilin-1, ~30% of cells displayed blebs with elongated necks (Figure 2A,D and Video 6).
evidence: This is supported by quantitative data in Figure 2D.

claim: ~60% of cells with elongated bleb necks display blebs that never retract into the cell body.
source: Detailed analyses of these cells revealed that ~60% display blebs that never retract into the cell body (Figure 2E).
evidence: This is supported by quantitative data in Figure 2E.

claim: Depleting lung adenocarcinoma A549 cells of both ADF and cofilin-1 results in the elongation of bleb necks.
source: Moreover, we found this effect to not be specific to melanoma A375 cells, as depleting lung adenocarcinoma A549 cells of both ADF and cofilin-1 similarly resulted in the elongation of bleb necks (Figure 2F–G).
evidence: This is supported by imaging and quantitative data in Figure 2F-G.

claim: Depleting both ADF and cofilin-1 had an additive effect on reducing the rate of bleb retraction.
source: In melanoma A375 cells, depleting both ADF and cofilin-1 had an additive effect on reducing the rate of bleb retraction, which points to these proteins having non-overlapping functions specifically at bleb necks (Figure 2H).
evidence: This is supported by quantitative data in Figure 2H.

claim: ADF and cofilin-1 have non-overlapping functions specifically at bleb necks.
source: In melanoma A375 cells, depleting both ADF and cofilin-1 had an additive effect on reducing the rate of bleb retraction, which points to these proteins having non-overlapping functions specifically at bleb necks (Figure 2H).
evidence: This is inferred from the additive effect on bleb retraction rate.

claim: In cells depleted of endogenous ADF and cofilin-1, EGFP-cofilin-1 is enriched at leader bleb necks.
source: In support of this role, we determined the location of EGFP-cofilin-1 in confined cells. Our initial efforts were unsuccessful because of a high degree of soluble (i.e., unbound to F-actin) protein, but in cells depleted of endogenous ADF and cofilin-1 we could detect an enrichment of EGFP-cofilin-1 at leader bleb necks (Figure 2I; arrow).
evidence: This is supported by imaging data in Figure 2I.

claim: A large concentration of F-actin is found at the necks of blebs in cells depleted of ADF and cofilin-1.
source: Thus far, our results suggest that ADF and cofilin-1 are important for the rapid turnover of cortical actin at bleb necks. In agreement with this concept, a large concentration of F-actin is found at the necks of blebs in cells depleted of ADF and cofilin-1 (Figure 3A).
evidence: This is supported by imaging data in Figure 3A.

claim: Migration plasticity is thought to be a major contributor of metastasis.
source: Because migration plasticity is thought to be a major contributor of metastasis, our aim here is to identify the essential factors required for the rapid cortical actin flow in leader blebs.
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge that motivates the study.

claim: Wiggan et al. reported an increase in the frequency of HeLa cells with blebs after cofilin-1 RNAi.
source: A similar elongated neck phenotype was observed by Wiggan et al., whereas they reported an increase in the frequency of HeLa cells with blebs after cofilin-1 RNAi (Wiggan et al., 2012).
evidence: This is supported by citation to prior work.

claim: Wiggan et al. contend that cofilin-1 inhibits contractility by competing with myosin for F-actin binding.
source: While these authors contend that cofilin-1 inhibits contractility by competing with myosin for F-actin binding, our results are in line with work showing that cofilin-1 increases contractility through optimizing actin filament lengths and de-branching (Chan et al., 2009; Chugh et al., 2017; Ennomani et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by citation to prior work.

claim: The current study's results are in line with work showing that cofilin-1 increases contractility through optimizing actin filament lengths and de-branching.
source: While these authors contend that cofilin-1 inhibits contractility by competing with myosin for F-actin binding, our results are in line with work showing that cofilin-1 increases contractility through optimizing actin filament lengths and de-branching (Chan et al., 2009; Chugh et al., 2017; Ennomani et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior work and the stiffness data in Figure 5A.

claim: Confined cells are placed under a slab of PDMS held at a defined height (~3 µm) above cover glass.
source: Using our previously described approach for cell confinement, which involves placing cells under a slab of PDMS held at a defined height (~3 µm) above cover glass, cancer cells will switch to LBBM (Figure 1A and Video 1; Logue et al., 2018).
evidence: This describes the experimental method used in the study.

claim: Cancer cells switch to LBBM when confined under PDMS at ~3 µm height.
source: Using our previously described approach for cell confinement, which involves placing cells under a slab of PDMS held at a defined height (~3 µm) above cover glass, cancer cells will switch to LBBM (Figure 1A and Video 1; Logue et al., 2018).
evidence: This is supported by imaging data in Figure 1A and Video 1, and citation to prior work.

claim: Myosin is concentrated at the leader bleb neck that separates the leader bleb from the cell body.
source: As indicated by an enrichment in EGFP tagged regulatory light chain (EGFP-RLC), we observe a concentration of myosin at the leader bleb neck that separates the leader bleb from the cell body (Figure 1C and Video 2; Liu et al., 2015; Ruprecht et al., 2015; Bergert et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by imaging data in Figure 1C and Video 2, and citations to prior work.
